paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses labeled and unlabeled examples together. When some classes are much more common than others, a classifier can favor those majority classes. Using its predictions on unlabeled data as additional training signals can reinforce that bias. This paper addresses how to use unlabeled examples while reducing that imbalance.

The proposed Auxiliary Balanced Classifier, or ABC, is a single layer attached to the representation learned by an existing semi-supervised model. It uses a class-balanced loss within each minibatch. Meanwhile, the underlying model learns representations from all examples in that minibatch, preserving information that could be lost by balancing the entire representation-learning process through selective data use.

ABC also adapts consistency regularization to use unlabeled data with equal selection probability across classes. Together, these choices separate learning useful features from training a balanced classifier. The authors report state-of-the-art results across class-imbalanced semi-supervised experiments on four benchmark datasets. Their findings support a lightweight addition to existing learning systems that addresses both biased predictions and the challenge of using unlabeled data effectively.
neurips-2021-abc-auxiliary-balanced-clas.tldr: ABC adds a lightweight balanced classifier to semi-supervised models to reduce majority-class bias while retaining useful information from unlabeled data.

paragraphs: This paper studies attacks on models that assign a label to an entire graph. That differs from attacking the classification of individual nodes, which has received more attention. Whole-graph classification matters in applications such as biochemistry and social network analysis, so understanding its vulnerabilities is a distinct problem with practical relevance.

The authors propose an attack based on Bayesian optimization. It works through black-box access, without requiring the internal model information assumed by some earlier methods. The method is designed to use relatively few queries and restrained graph perturbations. These properties address two practical obstacles to evaluating attacks: expensive repeated model access and the need to keep modifications limited.

Experiments examine graph classification tasks with different graph properties, constraints, and attack modes. The reported results support the method's effectiveness and flexibility across those evaluated settings. The authors also analyze recurring, interpretable patterns in the adversarial graphs they produce. Those patterns may help explain vulnerabilities in graph classifiers, although the abstract presents that explanatory role as a possibility rather than a complete account of robustness.
neurips-2021-adversarial-attacks-on-grap.tldr: A Bayesian optimization attack exposes graph-classifier vulnerabilities using black-box access, relatively few queries, and limited graph changes.

paragraphs: The paper studies label differential privacy: the trained model must provide a formal privacy guarantee for the labels attached to training examples. This specifies which part of the training data is protected. The authors develop two approaches and examine both their theoretical privacy guarantees and their behavior on standard benchmarks.

The first approach, ALIBI, combines additive Laplace noise with Bayesian inference. The authors argue that this combination suits typical machine-learning tasks better than the randomized-response mechanisms used in recent label-privacy methods. The second adapts the PATE framework using advances in semi-supervised learning. That adaptation can achieve very strong privacy levels in some regimes, a qualification central to the claim.

The evaluation also investigates memorization, providing an empirical perspective alongside formal guarantees. It suggests that ranking algorithms solely by their proven differential-privacy bounds can be misleading: a tighter analysis can make an algorithm look preferable even when empirical evaluation suggests weaker privacy. The contribution therefore includes both new learning methods and a warning about treating the tightness of a privacy analysis as a complete comparison of algorithms.
neurips-2021-antipodes-of-label-differen.tldr: Two label-private learning methods show promising results while highlighting that formal privacy bounds alone can give misleading algorithm comparisons.

paragraphs: When a function is random, the location of its maximum is also uncertain. The resulting distribution describes where the best point might be, rather than simply providing one optimum. This paper develops a general way to represent that distribution compactly through a set of optimized representative points, called centroids.

The method uses a simple objective to adjust those centroids without explicitly drawing exact samples from the distribution of maximizers. This matters because the desired representation can be constructed without making exact sampling an intermediate requirement. Under appropriate conditions, the authors show that the objective minimizes a surrogate for Wasserstein distance between the true distribution and its centroid approximation.

That theoretical result connects the optimization procedure to a measure of how closely two distributions match, while retaining the qualification that it concerns a surrogate under stated conditions. The paper demonstrates applications in few-shot image classification, personalized dialogue, and multi-target domain adaptation. These examples support the usefulness of the same compact distributional representation across several real-world multi-task learning settings.
neurips-2021-argmax-centroid-daa47d9259.tldr: Argmax centroid approximates a random function's distribution of maximizers with optimized representative points, without requiring exact samples from that distribution.

paragraphs: Causal discovery seeks a directed graph describing relationships among variables. Returning a single graph can hide uncertainty, particularly when observations are scarce or cannot uniquely identify the true causal structure. This paper develops BCD Nets to estimate a distribution over possible directed acyclic graphs within a linear-Gaussian structural equation model.

The approach uses variational inference to approximate that distribution. Graphs are discrete objects with many possible configurations, making Bayesian inference difficult to scale. The authors examine three design choices: an expressive family for representing candidate graph distributions, a continuous relaxation that supports low-variance stochastic optimization, and suitable prior distributions over the underlying latent variables.

These choices make uncertainty over causal graphs part of the learning target rather than reducing the result to one maximum-likelihood estimate. Experiments on real and synthetic data show better performance than maximum-likelihood methods on standard causal-discovery measures, including structural Hamming distance, when data are limited. The stated evidence supports the framework particularly in those low-data settings, where committing to one graph can obscure uncertainty in the inferred relationships.
neurips-2021-bcd-nets-scalable-variation.tldr: BCD Nets approximate distributions over causal graphs and outperform maximum-likelihood methods in the reported low-data experiments.

paragraphs: Reinforcement-learning agents must explore to discover rewarding behavior, but exploration methods with strong theoretical guarantees can be difficult to combine with flexible models such as neural networks. This paper focuses on that mismatch in least-squares value iteration, where established optimistic methods use upper confidence bounds to guide exploration.

BooVI is a bootstrapped variant of least-squares value iteration. It drives exploration through sampling and resampling, making the procedure compatible with general function approximators. The methodological contribution is therefore a different way to generate exploratory behavior that can fit a wider range of value-estimation models while retaining a rigorous analysis in a specific setting.

For episodic problems with linear function approximation, BooVI matches the stated worst-case regret bound of optimistic least-squares value iteration: roughly the square root of d³H³T, with logarithmic factors suppressed. Here d is feature dimension, H is episode length, and T is total interaction steps. The distinction matters: compatibility extends to general approximators, while the stated regret guarantee applies to the episodic linear setting.
neurips-2021-boovi-provably-efficient-bo.tldr: BooVI uses resampling to support flexible exploration while matching an established regret guarantee in episodic linear reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A video representation useful for classifying an entire clip may overlook the precise spatial and temporal details needed to locate an event. Conversely, features designed for localization may transfer poorly to broader recognition tasks. This paper addresses that split by learning representations intended to support both global meaning and fine-grained local information.

The method jointly optimizes two contrastive objectives using audio signals to encourage global and local visual learning. Rather than treating these objectives as independent training problems, it combines them within the same approach. The authors find that the objectives improve one another's generalizability, with jointly learned representations significantly outperforming the corresponding representations learned separately.

The evaluation spans action and sound classification, lipreading, deepfake detection, and event and sound localization. These tasks probe different demands on the learned features, from identifying what happens to locating relevant information. The findings support the idea that global and local objectives can be complementary: training for both can produce more broadly useful video representations than specializing each representation in isolation.
neurips-2021-contrastive-learning-of-glo.tldr: Joint audio-guided contrastive objectives learn video features that support both overall recognition and detailed localization better than separately learned counterparts.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks can model interactions among entities in videos, but building the graph requires deciding what each node represents. When the video supplies no explicit graph, earlier approaches commonly use pretrained object detectors or fixed regions. Those choices determine the elements whose interactions the network can learn.

This paper instead learns nodes that attach dynamically to clearly bounded, salient regions relevant to the higher-level task. It does so without object-level supervision. The localized, adaptive construction encourages an object-centered representation, while allowing the training task to influence which regions become graph nodes rather than fixing them in advance.

The authors show that the discovered regions correlate well with objects in the videos. That finding supports the intended object-centered bias without claiming that every learned node is a perfectly identified object. Ablation studies and experiments on two challenging datasets report better video-classification performance than previous graph neural network models. Together, the results connect the learned choice of graph elements with improved performance on the task those elements are meant to support.
neurips-2021-discovering-dynamic-salient.tldr: Learning adaptive video regions as graph nodes improves classification without requiring object-level supervision.

paragraphs: Wider neural networks have been associated with better adversarial-training performance, but this paper asks when extra width actually improves robustness. Its analysis separates accuracy on ordinary inputs from stability under perturbations. Robustness depends on their tradeoff, which is controlled by the strength of the robust regularization parameter, lambda.

With lambda held fixed, wider models can improve ordinary accuracy while becoming less stable to perturbations. Overall robustness can therefore worsen. The authors connect this instability to local Lipschitzness, which describes how sensitively network outputs change near an input. Using neural tangent kernel results, they theoretically show a tendency for wider networks to have worse perturbation stability.

This explains why tuning lambda on a small network and reusing it unchanged for a wider one can be problematic. The analysis indicates that increasing regularization appropriately is needed to realize the wider model's robustness potential. The proposed Width Adjusted Regularization method adaptively increases lambda for wide models and substantially reduces tuning time. The central finding is a relationship between width and regularization, rather than an unconditional advantage from adding width.
neurips-2021-do-wider-neural-networks-re.tldr: Wider networks can become less robust at fixed regularization, motivating an adaptive increase in regularization strength as width grows.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation trains a smaller student network to imitate a larger teacher, which may itself be an ensemble. The usual explanation is that the student benefits by reproducing the teacher's predictions. This paper investigates that explanation by separating two outcomes: matching the teacher and generalizing well to new data.

The authors find that distillation can improve student generalization even while the student's predictive distribution remains surprisingly different from the teacher's. Such discrepancies can persist when the student has enough capacity to match the teacher perfectly. They identify optimization difficulties as a key reason: having a model capable of representing the teacher does not ensure that training finds that representation.

The data used for distillation also influence how closely the student reproduces the teacher. Yet closer agreement does not always yield better generalization. This makes teacher imitation and student performance distinct measures of success. The results challenge a common account of why distillation works while preserving its practical benefit: a student can improve without faithfully copying the teacher, and better copying is not always better learning.
neurips-2021-does-knowledge-distillation.tldr: Knowledge distillation can improve generalization even when students poorly match their teachers, and closer matching does not always help.

paragraphs: Federated learning can expose information through shared gradients even when clients keep their original data private. Gradient inversion attacks attempt to reconstruct those inputs, at least partially, from gradient information. This paper evaluates existing attacks and defenses, focusing on how attack assumptions and protective measures affect the resulting privacy risk.

The authors find that some attacks rely on strong assumptions about the learning setup. Relaxing those assumptions can substantially reduce attack effectiveness. They also evaluate three proposed defenses and examine their tradeoffs between privacy leakage and data utility. Combining the defenses appropriately makes reconstruction less effective even when the attacks retain their original favorable assumptions.

The analysis additionally estimates the computational cost of recovering a single image from beginning to end under each evaluated defense. This adds a practical dimension to the comparison beyond whether reconstruction is possible. The findings suggest that the state-of-the-art attacks evaluated in the paper can be resisted with only minor utility loss. That conclusion concerns these assessed attacks and configurations, rather than establishing immunity to all possible gradient-based privacy attacks.
neurips-2021-evaluating-gradient-inversi.tldr: Evaluated gradient inversion attacks weaken under relaxed assumptions and suitable defense combinations, suggesting protection with minor data-utility loss.

paragraphs: Near out-of-distribution detection asks a model to recognize unfamiliar inputs that remain close to familiar data. This paper investigates whether large pretrained transformers improve that difficult distinction across data modalities. The authors report substantial gains in both image and genomics benchmarks, showing that the benefit extends beyond one type of input.

For CIFAR-100 versus CIFAR-10 detection, ImageNet21k-pretrained Vision Transformers raise AUROC from the reported previous best of 85% to over 96%. On a genomics benchmark, transformers with unsupervised pretraining increase AUROC from 66% to 77%. These results establish the paper's main empirical finding: large-scale pretraining can materially improve near-distribution detection in the evaluated settings.

The authors also study limited information about outliers. With one image per outlier class, image-detection AUROC reaches 98.7%; with ten, it reaches 99.46%. A separate approach uses image-text models such as CLIP with only outlier class names and no accompanying images. That approach also surpasses previous state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks, showing that textual descriptions can provide useful outlier information.
neurips-2021-exploring-the-limits-of-out.tldr: Pretrained transformers improve near out-of-distribution detection, with further gains from a few outlier images or even outlier class names.

paragraphs: Gradient-based optimization usually relies on information about how an objective changes with its parameters. This paper studies a constrained version of that process: the optimizer cannot directly inspect the complete output of its gradient oracle. Instead, it receives only information that survives a locally imposed restriction on access or processing.

The restrictions include local privacy requirements, gradient quantization, and computational limits that allow access to only a few gradient coordinates. These examples differ in motivation, but all limit what the optimizer can learn from a gradient. The paper asks about adaptivity in processing that output: whether the way restricted information is obtained can change as optimization proceeds.

The authors establish tight or nearly tight bounds for convex and strongly convex optimization when adaptive processing is permitted. Such bounds characterize the achievable limits of optimization under the information restrictions being studied. The contribution makes adaptivity part of the theoretical analysis instead of assuming a fixed processing procedure. The abstract does not assert that adaptive processing always helps; it reports a characterization of performance with adaptivity allowed.
neurips-2021-information-constrained-opt.tldr: The paper derives tight or nearly tight optimization bounds when gradients are accessed through adaptive, information-limited processing.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning starts with expert behavior and seeks a reward function that describes it. This can help when a useful reward is difficult to write manually, or when the aim is to infer an agent's preferences. The paper develops an algorithm for continuous state spaces where the transition dynamics are unknown.

A continuous state space allows states to vary across a continuum, rather than belonging to a finite list. Unknown dynamics mean that the algorithm is not given the system's transition behavior in advance. The authors model the system through a basis of orthonormal functions, providing a mathematical representation for addressing both aspects of this learning setting.

The contribution includes a correctness proof and formal bounds on sample requirements and running time. These guarantees address whether the algorithm works and how much data and computation it requires within its analyzed setting. Synthetic experiments corroborate the theoretical results. The paper thus connects reward inference from expert behavior with an explicitly analyzed algorithm for continuous systems, supported by controlled experimental evidence.
neurips-2021-inverse-reinforcement-learn.tldr: An inverse reinforcement-learning algorithm infers rewards in continuous state spaces with unknown dynamics and provides correctness and complexity guarantees.

paragraphs: Research on emergent communication asks how agents can develop ways to exchange information while solving tasks together. Much of that work uses sequences of discrete tokens as the communication channel. This paper investigates an alternative: agents communicate through drawings made from simple strokes, making the message itself a visual object.

The agents are neural networks, and their drawing procedure is differentiable. That allows training to connect the success of communication back to the process that creates the strokes. The authors study this setup through a referential communication game, where drawings carry information needed for the agents to refer successfully to the intended target.

The agents learn to communicate through drawing. With appropriate inductive biases, their drawings are also interpretable to humans. That qualification matters: successful communication between trained agents does not by itself establish human readability. The findings show that visual messages can support learned cooperation and, with suitable design choices, become accessible to people as well. The work motivates further study of drawing as a flexible communication channel for collaborative agents.
neurips-2021-learning-to-draw-emergent-c.tldr: Neural agents learn to communicate through simple drawings that humans can interpret when suitable inductive biases are used.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate an object's three-dimensional pose using a few labeled images and a larger unlabeled collection. The challenge is transferring pose information across previously unseen views and variations in shape, texture, lighting, and scene context. The proposed framework combines neural view synthesis with feature matching to make that transfer.

Objects are represented by three-dimensional cuboid meshes with feature vectors at their vertices. After initialization from labeled images, the model synthesizes feature representations for unseen viewpoints. Matching those representations against unlabeled images produces estimated pose labels. Those pseudo-labels then help train a feature extractor whose vertex features remain more consistent across different views.

Training alternates between improving the features and assigning poses to unlabeled data, following an EM-type procedure. On PASCAL3D+ and KITTI, the authors report large gains over all evaluated baselines, particularly with only seven annotated images. They also observe strong robustness to partial occlusion in out-of-distribution scenarios. The findings support a learning loop in which synthesized views and improved features help extend scarce pose annotations.
neurips-2021-neural-view-synthesis-and-m.tldr: Synthesizing and matching feature-based object views transfers scarce 3D pose labels to unlabeled images and improves few-shot pose estimation.

paragraphs: The paper studies what graph neural networks can approximate on latent-position random graphs as the graphs become very large. In this limit, ordinary GNNs converge to continuous counterparts. Analyzing these limiting models provides a way to investigate expressive power across random graph models rather than examining only individual finite graphs.

Without input node features, the continuous models can have severe limitations. They can fail to distinguish communities even in a well-separated stochastic block model with a constant degree function. The authors therefore study Structural GNNs, which augment networks with unique node identifiers. They establish convergence to continuous structural models under new conditions on those identifiers.

In the continuous limit, the structural models are strictly more expressive than ordinary continuous GNNs. The authors also prove universality for several graph families, including most stochastic block models and a large class of random geometric graphs. The results cover both graph-level outputs unchanged by node relabeling and node-level outputs that follow the relabeling. These guarantees concern the specified random graph families and limiting setting, rather than every possible finite graph.
neurips-2021-on-the-universality-of-grap.tldr: Under specified conditions, node identifiers make limiting graph neural networks more expressive and universal on several random graph families.

paragraphs: Very large gradients during variational autoencoder training can look like a numerical problem that should be eliminated. This paper asks what might be lost by forcing gradients to remain bounded. It examines a broad class of autoencoder objectives for data lying on or near a low-dimensional manifold, including natural-image data.

The analysis focuses on two competing failures. Excessive regularization can produce high reconstruction errors, sometimes described as posterior collapse. Insufficient regularization can leave unnecessary latent dimensions in the model. The authors prove that simultaneously avoiding both failures requires an energy function with infinite gradients around optimal representations, in the particular technical sense developed in their analysis.

The requirement is conditional on the studied setting and the joint goal of avoiding both forms of regularization error. It does not establish that every large gradient in every autoencoder is beneficial. Because these failures can harm generated samples or feature selection, the result suggests caution when modifying objectives merely to bound gradients. The paper argues that accommodating large gradients can sometimes preserve properties that such restrictions would remove.
neurips-2021-on-the-value-of-infinite-gr.tldr: Under the paper's technical conditions, avoiding both over- and under-regularization requires autoencoder objectives with infinite gradients near optimal representations.

paragraphs: Robust reinforcement learning seeks a policy with good worst-case performance across a set of possible environments. This paper considers model-free learning when that uncertainty set is unknown and centered on a misspecified environment that supplies the observations. The learner must therefore estimate the uncertainty set from samples while learning robust behavior.

The authors develop an estimation approach and two online, incremental algorithms: robust Q-learning for tabular problems and robust TDC for function approximation. Their convergence results differ in strength. Robust Q-learning converges to the optimal robust Q function, while robust TDC converges asymptotically to stationary points. The latter result does not claim convergence to a global optimum.

The analysis avoids additional discount-factor conditions required by the cited earlier result. Finite-time bounds also show convergence as fast as the corresponding standard algorithms, within a constant factor. Numerical experiments further support robustness. The authors explain that the approach can extend to other methods, including TD and SARSA, making sample-based uncertainty estimation a potentially reusable component of online robust learning.
neurips-2021-online-robust-reinforcement.tldr: Sample-based uncertainty estimation enables online robust reinforcement-learning algorithms with convergence guarantees and rates comparable to their standard counterparts.

paragraphs: Social-media filtering shapes which information people encounter and can influence their decisions. This paper examines how regulation of that filtering could be enforced, what compliance could cost a platform, and how an audit changes the content a platform is encouraged to select. It treats auditing and platform incentives as connected questions.

The authors propose a method that lets an auditor test compliance with a given regulation using only black-box access to the filtering algorithm. The auditor therefore does not need to inspect its internal implementation. The analysis then adopts the platform's perspective: maximizing its own objective while satisfying the regulatory constraint.

The paper identifies conditions under which compliance does not impose a high performance cost. This is a conditional result, rather than a claim that regulation is always inexpensive. It also finds that content diversity can help align platform and regulator interests. The contribution connects an externally applicable audit with an analysis of the behavior it incentivizes, showing why the composition of filtered content matters alongside the platform's objective.
neurips-2021-regulating-algorithmic-filt.tldr: A black-box auditing framework examines regulatory compliance and identifies conditions where content diversity helps align platform and regulator interests.

paragraphs: Event cameras and spiking neural networks offer a route toward low-power, low-latency perception, but learning complex continuous outputs remains challenging. This paper studies optical flow, the estimation of visual motion, using self-supervision. It also addresses a pipeline issue: a fully asynchronous system would require temporal information to accumulate inside the network.

The authors modify an existing artificial-neural-network training pipeline so its inputs encode minimal temporal information. They also reformulate the event-based optical-flow loss to improve its convexity. Using this pipeline, they compare recurrent artificial and spiking networks and investigate initialization, optimization, surrogate gradient shape, adaptive neuronal mechanisms, and learnable neuronal parameters.

Initialization and surrogate gradient width are crucial for learning from sparse inputs, while neuronal adaptivity and learnable parameters can improve performance. The proposed artificial and spiking networks achieve performance comparable to current artificial networks trained with self-supervision. These findings establish progress on learning and temporal integration for event-based motion estimation; the low-power and low-latency benefits motivate the work rather than constituting reported measurements in the abstract.
neurips-2021-self-supervised-learning-of.tldr: A revised self-supervised pipeline enables spiking networks to estimate event-based optical flow competitively, with initialization and surrogate gradients proving crucial.

paragraphs: This paper asks when observations of a non-uniform hypergraph can distinguish one community from multiple communities. It works within a broad degree-corrected mixed-membership framework. A central difficulty is that both hypotheses contain many unknown parameters, so the hardest one-community explanation depends on the particular multiple-community alternative being tested.

The authors propose a degree-matching strategy that uses tensor-scaling theory to construct a least favorable pair of hypotheses. The purpose is to identify competing explanations that are especially difficult to distinguish. This construction supports a standard minimax lower bound and a more informative characterization called a Region of Impossibility.

These results describe statistical barriers to successful testing rather than merely weaknesses of one algorithm. The paper also introduces a test that reaches the lower bound up to a logarithmic factor, showing that the impossibility results closely track achievable performance. Mixed memberships are discussed as well. Together, the lower bounds and the matching test clarify how far community detection through hypothesis testing can go in the studied hypergraph setting.
neurips-2021-sharp-impossibility-results.tldr: Degree matching yields sharp limits for testing hypergraph communities, with a proposed test attaining the lower bound up to a logarithmic factor.

paragraphs: Teaching an agent can require carefully designed rewards, expert demonstrations, or many small pieces of feedback. This paper explores richer, structured advice as another form of supervision. Its goal is to let an external teacher communicate useful guidance interactively and enable the learner to turn that guidance into skills.

The authors formalize decision-making problems in which several forms of teacher advice are available. Their learning algorithm has two stages: it first learns how to interpret advice, then learns from that advice to perform tasks. The resulting agent can complete tasks without continued human supervision, making advice a training resource rather than a permanent requirement during use.

Experiments cover puzzle solving, navigation, and locomotion. Agents trained with advice acquire new skills using significantly less human supervision than standard reinforcement-learning algorithms and often less than imitation learning. The comparison with imitation learning is therefore qualified rather than universal. The findings support structured advice as an information-rich teaching channel that can reduce the amount of human involvement needed in the evaluated interactive environments.
neurips-2021-teachable-reinforcement-lea.tldr: Agents that learn to interpret and use structured advice acquire skills with less human supervision in the evaluated interactive tasks.

paragraphs: Long-tailed recognition involves many classes with few examples and a smaller number of dominant classes. Training directly on that imbalance can favor common labels, weaken generalization, and produce poor calibration. This paper approaches the problem through class priors, connecting the frequency of labels to both data augmentation and the training loss.

The first method, Uniform Mixup or UniMix, adjusts how examples are selected and mixed to favor minority classes. The second, Bayias, addresses a bias attributed to inconsistent priors. Motivated by Bayesian reasoning, it compensates for that bias by modifying standard cross-entropy loss. The methods therefore intervene at different points: construction of training examples and evaluation of prediction errors.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical support for classification calibration with both methods. Experiments find better-calibrated models, and combining the techniques achieves state-of-the-art performance on CIFAR-LT, ImageNet-LT, and iNaturalist 2018. The results support addressing class imbalance through complementary changes to sampling, mixing, and loss design, rather than relying on ordinary training to overcome dominant-class preferences on its own.
neurips-2021-towards-calibrated-model-fo.tldr: Minority-oriented mixup and a prior-bias correction improve calibration and recognition performance on the reported long-tailed benchmarks.

paragraphs: Finding one kind of target among distractors can be easier than reversing their roles. This paper investigates that visual-search asymmetry with a model that receives a target and a search image, then generates eye movements until it finds the target. The model combines recognition that varies with viewing eccentricity and target-dependent guidance.

Across six classical search tasks showing human asymmetry, the model offers a plausible mechanism without prior exposure to the task stimuli or task-specific training. The authors then test whether the direction of asymmetry could arise from experience with natural images. They train the model on modified ImageNet data whose natural-image biases are removed or reversed.

Depending on the training protocol, the direction of search asymmetry disappears or changes. This supports the hypothesis that visual experience can shape the asymmetries exhibited by the model. The result shows how a classical perceptual property can emerge from the statistics of training data without dedicated search-task training. It provides a computational explanation consistent with human behavior, rather than establishing that humans necessarily acquire the bias through exactly the same mechanism.
neurips-2021-visual-search-asymmetry-dee.tldr: A visual-search model exhibits human-like asymmetries whose direction changes when biases in its visual training experience are removed or reversed.
